analysis.one_liner: Bars data brokers from selling lists of abuse survivors, crime victims, sick people, and officials.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2020 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for data brokers—companies that buy and resell personal information about people they have no direct relationship with—to sell lists of 'vulnerable populations': survivors of domestic, child, elder, and sexual abuse, stalking and trafficking victims, people diagnosed with diseases like HIV/AIDS, dementia, or genetic conditions, people in addiction treatment, people identified by their prescriptions, plus law enforcement officers and judges. The Federal Trade Commission would write rules to enforce the ban, and state attorneys general could sue violators in federal court on behalf of residents.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose safety depends on keeping sensitive facts out of other people's hands: abuse survivors whose addresses could be sold to their abusers, stalking and trafficking victims, people with diseases or addiction treatment records who could face discrimination or scams, and police officers and judges who could be targeted because of their jobs. The FTC and state attorneys general would get a new tool to go after brokers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Abuse survivors, crime victims, sick people, law enforcement

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a data broker to sell, license, trade, or make available for payment a 'vulnerable population list'—lists built from personal information about abuse survivors, crime and trafficking victims, people with diagnoses such as HIV/AIDS, genetic disease, or dementia, people identified by prescriptions or addiction treatment, and law enforcement officers and judges.

The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban the way it enforces other unfair and deceptive practices, including against nonprofits, and must issue final rules within one year of enactment; the ban takes effect when that rule is final or one year after enactment, whichever comes first.
State attorneys general could sue violators in federal court on behalf of their residents to stop the practice, force compliance, and win damages or restitution.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers lose the revenue from selling these sensitive lists, and any business or individual that bought them loses access to a ready-made target list. Compliance and legal risk fall on the data brokerage industry.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers selling sensitive personal lists

drawbacks.text: The bill only covers data brokers—businesses that sell personal information about people they have no direct relationship with—so a company selling its own customer lists, or information resold under the public-record carve-out, could still circulate much of the same data.
There is no private right of action: individuals harmed by an illegal sale could not sue on their own; enforcement depends on the FTC and state attorneys general acting.

The bill never specifies how a violation is proven: many of the banned lists are labeled inferences ('identified as having addictive behavior'), and no remedies, fines, or damages schedule is laid out beyond pointing to existing FTC and court mechanisms, so enforcement would depend heavily on FTC rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people covered—abuse survivors, stalking victims, people with stigmatized medical records—the benefit is concrete and potentially life-or-death: a sold list of domestic violence survivors' locations is a direct safety threat, and this removes the market for it. The cost falls entirely on a niche industry selling data no one can meaningfully consent to having sold. The main weakness is design: the carve-out for businesses selling their own data and the lack of a private right of action leave real gaps. On balance, a narrow, genuinely protective bill whose cost is small and whose benefit is large for the people named.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in December 2020, near the end of the Congress, and the committee never took it up; it died there in January 2021 with no hearing and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on December 2, 2020, in the final weeks of the 116th Congress.
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no further action was ever recorded.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the resale market for sensitive personal information: nothing changed, and they kept the legal ability to compile and sell lists of vulnerable people that the bill would have outlawed.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action—no hearing, no markup, no vote—before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican senator sponsored the bill and no one else—of either party—cosponsored or opposed it on the record, so no partisan split was ever tested.

industries.note: Brokers profit by compiling personal information about people they have no direct relationship with and reselling it; this bill would shut down their market for lists of abuse survivors, crime victims, people with diseases, and law enforcement and judicial officials. Their interest in selling these lists runs directly against the safety of the people listed.

Firms that buy targeting lists would lose access to pre-built audiences of vulnerable people—patients, addicts, trauma survivors—whose data is valuable precisely because it identifies people in a weakened or exploitable position.
